source_text: Audi sane ubi vim humanae libertatis ostendit: Ego veni in nomine Patris mei, et non suscepistis me; si alius venerit in nomine suo, illum accipietis [n218] . Et item: Aut facite arborem bonam, et fructum eius bonum; aut facite arborem malam, et fructum eius malum [n219] . Et item: Si mihi non vultis credere, operibus credite [n220] . Atque omnibus vehementius, quod dicit intentionem suam humana voluntate impeditam fuisse: Hierusalem, inquit, Hierusalem, quoties volui congregare filios tuos, sicut gallina pullos suos sub alas suas, et noluisti! [n221] Post quod non sequitur: Sed te nolente collegi; verum: Relinquetur vobis domus vestra deserta [n222] ; ut illos ostendat pro malo quidem opere iure puniri, sed ab intentione propria non debuisse ulla necessitate revocari. Sic enim et per Prophetam locutus erat: Si volueritis, et audieritis me, quae bona sunt terrae comeditis; si nolueritis, et non audieritis, gladius vos comedet [n223] . Quomodo ergo tu liberum arbitrium non negas, quod non quidem sermone tuo, sed Evangelii testimonio, sensu autem tuo, non liberum pronuntiasti?
pass_a_gloss: Hear indeed where he shows the force of human liberty: I came in the name of my Father, and you did not take me up; if another shall have come in his own name, you will receive him. And likewise: Either make a tree good, and its fruit good; or make a tree evil, and its fruit evil. And likewise: If you are unwilling to believe me, believe the works. And more vehemently than all, that he says his intention was impeded by human will: Jerusalem, he says, Jerusalem, how often I willed to gather your sons, as a hen her chicks under her wings, and you were unwilling! After which it does not follow: But with you unwilling I gathered; but: Your house will be left to you deserted; that he may show those indeed to be punished by right for an evil work, but that they ought not to have been called back from their own intention by any necessity. For thus he had also spoken through the Prophet: If you shall have willed, and shall have heard me, you will eat the good things of the land; if you shall have been unwilling, and shall not have heard, the sword will eat you. How therefore do you not deny free choice, which not indeed by your speech, but by a testimony of the Gospel, but by your sense, you pronounced not free?

pass_b_english: Listen to where he shows the power of human freedom: “I came in my Father's name, and you did not receive me. If another comes in his own name, you will receive him” (John 5:43). And again: “Either make the tree good and its fruit good, or make the tree bad and its fruit bad” (Matthew 12:33). And again: “If you are unwilling to believe me, believe the works” (John 10:38). Most forcefully of all, he says that his intention was hindered by human will: “Jerusalem, Jerusalem, how often I wanted to gather your children as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, and you were unwilling!” (Matthew 23:37). He does not then add, “But I gathered you against your will.” Rather: “Your house will be left to you desolate” (Matthew 23:38). Thus he shows that they are rightly punished for their evil action, but ought not to have been forced away from their own intention by any compulsion. In the same way he had spoken through the prophet: “If you are willing and listen to me, you will eat the good things of the land. If you are unwilling and do not listen, the sword will devour you” (Isaiah 1:19–20). How, then, do you not deny free choice, when you pronounced it unfree, not indeed in your own wording but through the Gospel's testimony as interpreted by you?

choices.why: Julian's definition of sin is an act of will. Keep 'will' rather than later 'free will' system language unless liberum arbitrium is present.
Glossary default: arbitrium is the decision-power, not a later Augustinian/Reformation free-will locus.
